title: Why you do it
hook: self-determination theory: we persist longer when motivation comes from within (Deci and Ryan)

segments.voice: Yesterday, someone who, and the line I'm someone who. Did you finish the sentence? Today we dig underneath it, to the reason that holds it up. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-four.

A doctor's advice, written on a slip of paper: sit quietly for two minutes a day. Down the hall, someone else sits for the same two minutes because the quiet helps them be gentler at home. Same posture, same timer, same bell. From the outside, nothing tells them apart. The difference only shows up if someone asks a single question: why are you doing this? Two psychologists built a whole theory around that question, and it sorts these two sitters in a way that matters.
screen: `SAME TWO MINUTES.` → `TWO DIFFERENT REASONS.` → `ONE QUESTION: WHY?`

segments.voice: First, the theory. Edward Deci and Richard Ryan built what they call self-determination theory. Its starting point: motivation isn't one thing with a volume knob. It comes in kinds. Some reasons feel imposed from outside: a reward, a threat, someone watching. Some feel like your own. In their research, the second kind tends to go with sticking at things longer and getting more out of them. Second, the middle ground. People sometimes hear this as only do what's fun. The theory says something more useful. Between pure pressure and pure enjoyment sit reasons you've made your own: I don't love every sit, but I value what it does. Deci and Ryan put that kind, a value you've taken in and agree with, on the side of the self. A reason doesn't have to be pleasant to be yours. Third, the guilt trap. They also describe reasons that live inside your head but still work like pressure: I should, I'll feel bad if I skip. Those come from within and still feel imposed. Guilt can get someone to the cushion for a while; the theory treats it as a shakier engine than a value they actually hold. Fourth, an older voice. The philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche wrote, roughly, that someone who has their own why can bear almost any how. He wasn't writing about habits. But the shape fits: a reason you own makes the dull days easier to carry.
screen: `MOTIVATION COMES IN KINDS.` · `A REASON YOU'VE MADE YOUR OWN.` · then, large: `'I SHOULD' IS STILL PRESSURE.` · then: `A WHY CAN BEAR A HOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your inner reason. Not the reason you'd give at a party, and not one that starts with 'I should.' Ask quietly: when this practice goes well, what does it give me, or the people around me? Let an answer come in a few words. Calmer mornings. Patience with my mother. A minute that's mine. Hold that reason for a breath or two. Then let it rest, and sit with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Why you do it. The kind of reason behind a practice matters: a reason you own tends to outlast pressure and guilt. Today's word.

Your line: my own reason. Today, when you catch an 'I should' in your head, check whether a reason of your own is hiding underneath it, and try saying that one instead. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: People who draw on self-determination theory often write down, in their own words, what a practice gives them, and return to that reason on days when the practice feels like an obligation.

fork.setup: a friend says she sits every morning 'because I'm supposed to.' what would self-determination theory listen for next?
options: whether a reason of her own sits underneath.
whether someone checks up on her.
fork.reveal: the theory cares about the kind of reason: a value she holds herself tends to last longer than 'supposed to.'

trapdoor: what you thought: motivation is just how badly you want it.
what it means: the kind of reason matters, and reasons you own tend to last longer.
what a scholar hears: self-determination theory runs from external to integrated motivation, and counts guilt-driven 'introjected' reasons as controlled.

notes: The index hook says 'we persist longer'; the script says 'in their research, the second kind tends to go with sticking at things longer' to avoid a universal claim. Confirm against Ryan & Deci.
Confirm the summary of the continuum: external, introjected (guilt/should), identified and integrated, intrinsic; identified/integrated counted as autonomous.

Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows 12, paraphrased ('if we have our own why of life...'); no translation quoted. The line is often credited to Viktor Frankl, who quoted Nietzsche; the script credits Nietzsche.
The practice ('name your inner reason') is from the outline.
